hints: A tree has either one center or two adjacent centers.
An isomorphism must map centers to centers.
Assign each rooted subtree a canonical ID based on its sorted child IDs.
analogy: Compare family trees from their middle, ignoring the order in which siblings are drawn.
example: The paths 1-2-3 and 1-3-2 both have a central vertex with two leaf children, so they are isomorphic.
algorithm: Find each tree center by repeatedly removing leaves. Root each tree at a center and compute canonical subtree IDs bottom-up: sort the child IDs and intern that vector in one shared dictionary. If there are two centers, either compare both possible root choices or connect a virtual root to the two centers after removing their connecting edge. The trees are isomorphic exactly when their canonical root IDs match.
correctness: Leaf removal identifies the center set, which every tree isomorphism preserves. Two rooted subtrees have the same canonical ID exactly when their multisets of child subtree IDs match, by induction from leaves. Trying the center choices therefore covers every possible unrooted isomorphism.
complexity: For n vertices, sorting child IDs and dictionary operations take O(n log n) time and O(n) space per test, with shared interning of vectors.
